paragraphs: In the previous classes we have studied that similar charges repel and opposite charges attract each other with a force, known as force of interaction. There are two different kinds of charges, which are called positive and negative charges. Electrons have a negative charge and protons have positive charge.

The atom is electrically neutral. In SI units, charge is measured in coulombs (symbol C). The charge carried by an elementary particle is written as e, and its magnitude is |e| = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The important characteristic of the charge is that charge is quantized. Quantization of charge means that it exists in discrete packets. Charge q is an integral multiple of minimum elementary charge e, i.e., q = ne (11.1).

For your information (p. 3). When you charge up your body by touching the Van de Graaff generator your hair stands on end. The hair stands because all hair gains the same electric charge and repel each other. The force of repulsion is so great that it exceeds the weight of each hair strand. Your arms do not lift away from your body though — even they have the same charge as your body. This is because they are too heavy!

Here we make quantitative analysis of the nature of these forces. We would like to determine the magnitude and direction of such forces. The quantitative measurement of the force between two electric charges was first made by Coulomb (1736–1805). He carried out series of experiments to measure the force between electric charges using an apparatus known as torsion balance. Coulomb expresses his experimental data in the form of a statement which is known as Coulomb’s law.

It states “The magnitude of the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.” The magnitude of the force F between two electric charges q₁ and q₂ separated by distance r can be expressed as F ∝ q₁q₂ (A), F ∝ 1/r² (B). Combining Eq. (A) & Eq. (B), F ∝ q₁q₂/r², F = kq₁q₂/r² (11.2).

Here k is a constant of proportionality and its value depends upon the system of the units used and the medium between the charges. The electric charges q₁ and q₂ are assumed to be point or localized charges, provided the size of the bodies carrying the charges is very small as compared to the distance between them.

Figure 11.1. Coulomb force between (a) similar charges and (b) opposite charges. In order to show the direction of the force we use unit vector along the line joining the two charges. In fig. 11.1(a), r̂₁₂ is unit vector, pointing from the charge q₁ towards the charge q₂. The force on charge q₂ due to charge q₁ is F⃗₂₁ = k(q₁q₂/r²)r̂₁₂ (11.3a). For like charges the product q₁q₂ will be positive and the force is repulsive. Similarly for unlike charges the product q₁q₂ will be negative and the force is attractive.

Similarly the unit vector r̂₂₁ points from the charge q₂ towards the charge q₁. The force on charge q₁ due to q₂ is F⃗₁₂ = k(q₁q₂/r²)r̂₂₁ (11.3b). Since r̂₁₂ = −r̂₂₁, from Eq. 11.3(a) and 11.3(b) we can write F⃗₂₁ = −F⃗₁₂ (11.4). F⃗₂₁ is the force exerted by q₁ on q₂ and F⃗₁₂ is the force exerted by q₂ on q₁. Eq. 11.4 shows that the two forces are the same in magnitude but opposite in direction, as illustrated in fig. 11.1(b).
The constant k can be expressed in terms of the permittivity of free space ε₀, i.e., k = 1/(4πε₀). Experimentally measured value of ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², so k = 1/(4πε₀) = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².

Coulomb’s law in material media. Eq. (11.2) gives the force between two charges when there is air or vacuum between them. It is experimentally observed that when an insulator is placed between the electric charges, it reduces the force. Permittivity is the property of a medium which affects the magnitude of force between two point charges. Coulomb’s force can now be written as Fₘₑd = q₁q₂/(4πεr²) (11.5).

The quantity ε is called the permittivity of the medium. The permittivity of a material medium compared with the permittivity of vacuum is called relative permittivity or dielectric constant εᵣ for a particular insulator. Its ratio is given by εᵣ = ε/ε₀ (11.6). The dielectric constant is dimensionless. The values for the insulating materials in the table exceed unity.

Table 11.1. Relative permittivity of various dielectrics. Vacuum 1, air 1.0006, benzene 2.284, “Germinium” [printed spelling] 16, water 78.5, glass 4.8–10, mica 3–7.5, paraffin paper 2, rubber 2.94 and liquid ammonia 22–25.
The force in a medium of relative permittivity εᵣ is given by F⃗ₘₑd = (1/4πε₀εᵣ)(q₁q₂/r²)r̂ (11.7). Fₘₑd = Fᵥₐc/εᵣ (11.8).

Editorial clarification. In the scalar magnitude equations (11.2) and (11.5), use |q₁q₂|. Keep the signed product in the vector equations. The model assumes point charges in an effectively infinite homogeneous isotropic medium. The source approximates air as vacuum. For ordinary isolated bodies n is an integer, with its sign giving the sign of the charge. The printed life dates end in 1805. The Bibliothèque nationale de France records Coulomb’s death in 1806.

Related exercise. Numerical problem 1, p. 57, asks for the attraction between an iron nucleus of charge +26e and an electron at a separation of 1 × 10⁻¹² m. With the printed rounded constants, F = 9.0 × 10⁹ × 26 × (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)²/(10⁻¹²)² = 5.9904 × 10⁻³ N, consistent with the printed answer 6 × 10⁻³ N.

Before we start to define electric flux we start with area A and we take it as a vector quantity. As you may recall in chapter two (class 11), area is a geometric representation of a vector product. In this context A⃗ is a vector whose magnitude is equal to the surface area and whose direction is normal to the surface.

The electric flux Φ for uniform field E⃗ and area A⃗ is described in the text as the number of lines of force that pass through the area placed in the electric field. Φ = E⃗ · A⃗ = EA cos θ (11.11). Thus flux Φ is the scalar product of the electric field and the plane surface area. Figure 11.11(a) illustrates this by counting six lines passing through a surface. The electric flux depends upon the orientation of the area with respect to the field lines.

Flux at any angle. When the area vector makes an angle θ with the electric field lines as in fig. 11.11(b), the flux is Φ = EA cos θ. The area presented perpendicularly to the field contributes the factor A cos θ.

Maximum flux. If the surface is placed perpendicular to the electric field such that the area vector is parallel to E⃗, the maximum number of electric lines of force will pass through the surface. Consequently the electric flux is maximum, Φ = EA cos 0° = EA. Figure 11.11(c) shows this orientation.

Zero flux. If the surface is placed parallel to the electric field such that A⃗ is normal to E⃗, no electric lines of force will pass through the surface. Then Φ = EA cos 90° = 0, as in fig. 11.11(d).

Electric flux through a closed surface. If the field is nonuniform or the surface is curved, divide the surface into very small patches of area ΔA called differential areas. Assume these are approximately flat and so small that the electric field is almost uniform over each one. For one patch the flux contribution is approximately E⃗ · ΔA⃗. To calculate the total flux through the whole surface we add the flux from each patch, Φ ≈ Σ E⃗ · ΔA⃗.

Consider a closed surface of arbitrary shape. The positive normal is taken to be outward from the enclosed volume. If ΔA is the magnitude of the differential area and n̂ is the unit normal in the positive direction, the vector area is ΔA⃗ = ΔA n̂. Figure 11.12(a) shows the area normal and the radial field around a charge. Figure 11.12(b) shows a bundle of field lines passing through a closed surface.

For a closed surface the flux may be positive, negative or zero. (i) Flux is positive if the net number of field lines is leaving the surface. There is a net source inside. (ii) Flux is negative if more field lines enter than leave the surface. There is a net sink inside. (iii) Flux is zero if the numbers entering and leaving are equal or if no field line crosses the surface.

Editorial clarification. Drawn field lines illustrate flux with an arbitrary drawing density. Six drawn lines do not specify six SI units. The signed flux has units N m²/C. A crossed-through printed sentence on p. 20 says field lines are parallel to the area and do not intersect the surface. This is a special case for a field tangent to the surface, whereas fig. 11.12(b) shows lines crossing twice. In the limit of vanishing patch size, the sum becomes the surface integral ∮ E⃗ · dA⃗.

Electronic flashguns for cameras have to be left for a short period of time between flashes. There is a capacitor inside that stores energy. It needs to be charged up again by the battery in the flashgun. The time taken for this depends on the rate at which the charge is flowing, which in turn is determined by the resistance of the circuit. It can take a couple of seconds before the capacitor is effectively fully charged.

Figure 11.35 shows a resistor–capacitor circuit called an RC circuit. When switch S is closed to connect the upper circuit, a battery of voltage V starts charging the capacitor through the resistor R. The charge builds up gradually on the plates to the maximum value of q₀. Suppose at t = 0 the charge on the capacitor is zero. As charge builds up on the plates, the current drops. Charging stops in the limiting state where the potential difference between the plates equals the electromotive force of the battery.

Maximum charge on capacitor = capacitance × e.m.f. of battery. Experiments show that the charging process exhibits exponential behavior, q = q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)) (11.41). Here e is a constant with approximate value 2.7182. The graph of time t and charge q starts at q = 0 at t = 0 and increases gradually toward q₀. Figure 11.36 shows the growth of charge for small and large RC.

Time constant. The time taken to charge a capacitor in a given circuit is determined by the time constant of the circuit. The bigger the capacitance, the longer it takes to charge the capacitor. The larger the resistance, the smaller the current, which also increases the charging time. The factor RC is called the time constant. In one time constant 63.2% of the maximum charge is deposited on the plates.

For your information (p. 49). In principle, a capacitor can never charge up fully, because the rate of charging decreases as the charge increases. In practice, after a finite time the charging current becomes too small to measure, and the capacitor is effectively fully charged.

Putting t = RC in eq. (11.41) gives q = q₀(1 − e⁻¹) ≈ q₀(1 − 1/2.718) ≈ 0.632q₀, so q/q₀ ≈ 63.2% (11.42). The graph also shows that the charge approaches its maximum sooner when the time constant is small.

Figure 11.37 illustrates the discharging of a charged capacitor through a resistor. When the switch is closed, charge flows through the resistance, neutralizing the opposite charges on the plates. Assuming the initially fully charged capacitor begins discharging at t = 0, the magnitude of charge left on either plate at time t is q = q₀e^(−t/RC) (11.43).

The graph in fig. 11.38 shows that discharging begins at t = 0 with q = q₀ and that q decreases gradually toward zero. Smaller values of RC lead to a more rapid discharge. When t = RC, the text prints q = 0.367q₀ and q/q₀ = 36.7% (11.44).

The charging and discharging of a capacitor has many applications. Capacitor discharge ignition (CDI) is a type of automotive electronic ignition system used in motorcycles, lawn mowers, chain saws, small engines, turbine-powered aircraft and some cars. It was developed to overcome the long charging times associated with high-inductance coils in inductive ignition systems, making ignition more suitable for high engine speeds in small, racing and rotary piston engines. The text describes a stronger spark. Figure 11.39 shows an electronic ignition coil.

Editorial corrections. At t = RC, e⁻¹ ≈ 0.367879, giving 36.8% at one decimal place. Page 49 refers to fig. 11.35 for the charging graph, whose printed caption is fig. 11.36. Figure 11.35 shows current arrows reversed relative to the battery’s positive terminal for conventional charging current. Figure 11.37 repeats a battery in the discharge loop, and the prose reverses the marked plate signs. Free discharge in eq. (11.43) requires the battery to be disconnected and the resistor to be connected across the capacitor.

Related exercises. Conceptual questions 11 and 12 on p. 57 ask why the resistor voltage drops during charging and how to sketch capacitor voltage versus time in both modes. Since V_R = iR and i decreases during charging, V_R decreases. Since V_C = q/C, the capacitor voltage curves have the same shapes as the corresponding charge curves.
